summary: Specifies how to set up and maintain pseudowires with the Label Distribution Protocol, emulating Layer 2 services such as Ethernet over an MPLS network. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: A pretend cable carried through a bigger network, so two far-apart sites seem plugged together.

questions: how does ldp set up a pseudowire
what is the pwid fec element
what is the control word in a pseudowire
subtitle: How two edge routers use LDP to agree on the label that carries an emulated Layer 2 link across an MPLS network.

tldr.problem: Layer 2 services such as Frame Relay, ATM and Ethernet can be carried over an MPLS backbone on pseudowires, but the two edge routers need a way to agree on which label identifies which pseudowire and what state it is in.
tldr.mechanism: The routers set up an LDP session and exchange Label Mapping messages whose FEC identifies the pseudowire, using either the PWid FEC (type 0x80) or the Generalized PWid FEC (type 0x81). A PW Status TLV and Notification messages then report the pseudowire's health.
tldr.outcome: This is the Internet Standard version of the procedures from RFC 4447, and it also obsoletes RFC 6723 by adding control-word renegotiation. The RFC says the technology was first deployed in 2001.

today: RFC 8077 is an Internet Standard, and it obsoletes RFC 4447 and RFC 6723. The RFC reports that pseudowire technology was first deployed in 2001 and that every feature in the specification has been implemented by multiple vendors.

sections.title: Pseudowires and the Role of LDP
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) emulates a Layer 2 service such as Frame Relay, ATM or Ethernet over an MPLS-enabled network. Other documents say how to wrap a Layer 2 frame; this RFC says how the two ends of the pseudowire set it up and keep track of it using the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

The packet sent on a pseudowire carries a demultiplexer field in front of the encapsulated frame. In this protocol that field is an MPLS label, so the packets crossing the network are MPLS packets. They travel through a packet switched network (PSN) tunnel, which can be an MPLS LSP or any other tunnel that can carry MPLS packets. Setting up that tunnel is out of scope.

Only point-to-point pseudowires are covered. Point-to-multipoint, multipoint-to-point and QoS issues are explicitly not discussed. The two edge routers are called PE1 (ingress) and PE2 (egress), and the customer devices connect to them over attachment circuits (ACs).
sections.eli5: A pseudowire is a pretend cable running through a big shared network. LDP is how the two ends of the pretend cable talk to each other and agree how to use it.

sections.title: The Pseudowire Label
sections.content:
The design rests on one idea. Many pseudowires can share a single MPLS tunnel, so the network core never has to keep state for individual pseudowires. When PE2 receives a packet, it looks at the PW label to learn that the packet came over a pseudowire and which one. For an ATM payload that label maps to a particular virtual circuit, for Frame Relay to a DLCI value, and for Ethernet to an outgoing interface and perhaps a VLAN identifier.

PE1 puts the PW label on the packet first. If the tunnel is an MPLS LSP, it then pushes a tunnel label on top. The PW label is therefore always at the bottom of the label stack and is not visible again until the packet reaches PE2. Labels MUST be allocated from the per-platform label space.

The process is one-way, so it is repeated independently for each direction. LDP MUST exchange PW FEC label bindings in downstream unsolicited mode, and liberal label retention SHOULD be used. Static assignment of PW labels is also allowed, and implementations SHOULD support it.

A receiving LSR MUST answer a Label Request with either a Label Mapping or a Notification explaining why not. This is stricter than the LDP base specification, RFC 5036.
sections.eli5: Lots of pretend cables share one big road. Each parcel gets a sticker number so the receiving post office knows which pretend cable it belongs to.

sections.title: The PWid and Generalized PWid FEC Elements
sections.content:
The two PEs set up an LDP session using Extended Discovery. A Label Mapping message carries a FEC TLV, which says what the label means, and a Label Mapping for a pseudowire MUST contain exactly one FEC element and use the Generic Label TLV. Two FEC elements are defined, and only one is used per pseudowire.

The PWid FEC element (type 0x80) is used when both ends are provisioned with the same 32-bit identifier. It carries the C-bit, a 15-bit PW type, a PW info length, a 32-bit Group ID, a non-zero 32-bit PW ID and optional Interface Parameter Sub-TLVs. The PW ID and PW type MUST match at both ends. Each endpoint starts its own unidirectional LSP, and the two are bound into one pseudowire when the PW ID and PW type agree.

The Generalized PWid FEC element (type 0x81) is for cases where the far end must be discovered rather than statically configured. It names the endpoints with an Attachment Group Identifier (AGI), a Source AII (SAII) and a Target AII (TAII), each carried as a type, a length and a value. Unused sub-elements are sent with length 0. Group ID and interface parameters move into separate optional TLVs: the PW Group ID TLV and the PW Interface Parameters TLV.

Because the Interface Parameter Sub-TLV is part of the FEC, it cannot change once the pseudowire is up, so it must not carry changing information such as status.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to name a pretend cable. One is a plain number both sides already know. The other is a longer address label for when one side has to figure out who is on the other end.

sections.title: Setting Up a Generalized PW
sections.content:
With the Generalized PWid FEC, the egress PE that already knows its peer starts setup by sending a Label Mapping message containing the AGI, SAII and TAII. The receiving PE treats this as a request to set up a pseudowire whose endpoint is the forwarder identified by the TAI. How it maps that identifier to a forwarder is a local matter.

If the receiver cannot map the TAI to one of its forwarders, it sends a Label Release with the status code Unassigned/Unrecognized TAI. If it accepts, it makes sure a pseudowire LSP exists in the opposite direction, sending its own Label Mapping with the source and target identifiers reversed if it has not already done so.

A bidirectional pseudowire is therefore two LSPs, where the FEC of one has the SAII and TAII reversed relative to the other.
sections.eli5: One side calls the other and says who it wants to reach. If the other side knows who that is, it calls back with the names swapped, and now the line works both ways.

sections.title: Signaling Pseudowire Status
sections.content:
PEs MUST send Label Mapping messages as soon as the PW is configured and administratively enabled, whatever the state of the attachment circuit. The label should be withdrawn only if the operator configures the pseudowire down or deletes it. A simple label withdrawal MAY still be supported as a legacy way to signal status.

The richer method is the PW Status TLV (type 0x096A), a 4-octet bit field. Each bit can flag a different fault, and a fault is cleared by sending a Notification with that bit cleared. The lowest bit, PW Not Forwarding, is only a generic failure indication for link-down events that no other bit covers. Updates travel in an LDP Notification message with status code 0x00000028 and a Message ID of 0.

Support is negotiated at setup. A PE that supports the TLV MUST include it in its initial Label Mapping. If the remote side does not send one back, both fall back to the label withdraw method. Peers that do not understand the TLV ignore it because its I bit is set.

A PE can also send one wildcard status notification, with the PW info length set to 0 and only the Group ID or PW Group ID TLV present, to report a change for every affected pseudowire. All PEs are REQUIRED to accept this but are not required to send it.
sections.eli5: The two ends keep sending little notes saying whether their end of the pretend cable is working. If one side cannot read the notes, they use the older way: taking the number away entirely.

sections.title: The Control Word and C-bit Negotiation
sections.content:
The control word is an optional field between the label stack and the payload. The C-bit in the FEC says whether it is in use: 1 means present, 0 means absent. For PW types that require it, Label Mapping messages MUST have C=1, and a received C=0 is answered with a Label Release carrying an Illegal C-bit status, so that PW is not enabled.

For other types, each endpoint MUST be configurable as PREFERRED or NOT PREFERRED, with a default that the RFC does not choose. If a mapping with C=1 arrives and the local side does not prefer the control word, it replies by advertising its own preference. If the peer's C=0 reaches a side that sent C=1, that side sends a Label Withdraw with a Wrong C-bit code and then a mapping with C=0. The result is that the control word is used only if both ends prefer it.

Section 7.3, added in this RFC (and the reason RFC 6723 is obsoleted), covers renegotiation after re-provisioning. The local PE withdraws and releases the label, sends a Label Request and waits for the peer's Label Mapping, and SHOULD NOT interrupt the process before it finishes.
sections.eli5: Both sides have to agree whether to add an extra label strip to each parcel. If either side says no, they skip it, and they can talk it over again if someone changes their mind later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC separates the data plane and the control plane. For the data plane, the pseudowire encapsulations alone do not let the receiver authenticate the sender, assure the packet was not altered, or keep it private. The MPLS network SHOULD be isolated so that outsiders cannot insert MPLS packets, and it should not accept MPLS packets from external interfaces unless the top label was legitimately distributed to the sender.

For the control plane, an incoming LDP session request MUST NOT be accepted unless its source address belongs to an eligible peer, and source address spoofing must be prevented some other way. The LDP MD5 authentication option from RFC 5036 MUST be implemented and, for more security, used. It gives integrity and authentication but not privacy, and because it relies on pre-shared keys it offers little protection against replay attacks.
sections.eli5: Only post offices you already trust may join the conversation, and each message carries a secret stamp so nobody can pretend to be a trusted office.
